h1: The 6 Best Bluetooth Tracker Sets Under $100 for Families and Travelers, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 Bluetooth trackers and multi-packs under $100 from Apple, Samsung, Tile, Chipolo and UGREEN, matched to your phone.
summary: The Apple AirTag (2nd Generation) 4-pack is the best set for iPhone households, since it brings four tags and the Find My network to the under $100 bracket. The Samsung Galaxy SmartTag2 is the best match for Android 11 phones and tablets, the Tile Essentials set suits mixed families, and the UGREEN Finder Duo Air 4-pack is a cross-platform multi-pack for people who want volume. Skip the imported Samsung 4-pack unless you accept its missing US warranty.
intro: A bigger budget does not make the phone question go away. At under $100 you can buy a four-pack or a mixed bundle, and the most common error is filling a drawer with tags that talk to a network your phone cannot reach. Count your devices and your family's before you count your keychains.

This ranking is built for buyers who want several tags at once. We reviewed six sets and single tags using the maker listings, covering compatibility, pack size, water resistance and battery claims. We ranked by how well each fits a real household, and we flag when a listing leaves out a detail such as warranty coverage or network size.

products.name: Apple AirTag (2nd Generation) 4 Pack
products.verdict: Four second-generation AirTags with a longer finding range and the Find My network behind them.
products.description:
This listing is the four-pack of Apple's second-generation AirTag, sold in the $50 to $100 bracket. The listing highlights up to 1.5X the precision finding range of the first model, a built-in sound and one-tap setup with an iPhone or iPad.

It ranks first because it combines the biggest finding network with enough tags to cover keys, a backpack, a suitcase and a laptop sleeve. Find My relies on the vast number of Apple devices around you, so a tag left behind in a public place can still report its location. The weakness is lock-in: nothing here works with Android, and a family with mixed phones will leave someone out.

It is the right buy for an iPhone family that wants to tag everything important in one purchase. Skip it if even one person who needs tracking carries an Android phone.
pros: Four tags cover a whole household
Find My network has huge reach
products.idealFor: iPhone families tagging keys, bags and luggage.
products.skipIf: Anyone who needs tracking uses Android.

products.name: Samsung Galaxy SmartTag2 Bluetooth Tracker
products.verdict: A single Samsung tag for Android 11 or later phones and tablets, with item and pet use in mind.
products.description:
The Galaxy SmartTag2 is Samsung's Bluetooth tracker for keys, wallets, luggage and pets, designed for phones and tablets on Android 11 or later. The single-tag listing here costs between $25 and $50.

Second place goes to it since Android owners have few polished options, and this is the one that fits the Galaxy ecosystem naturally. A single tag also lets you try the system before buying a bigger set. It is below the AirTag four-pack because Samsung's network depends on Galaxy devices nearby, so coverage is thinner away from other users of its phones. The listing also needs an Android 11 phone, which rules out older handsets.

Buy it if you have a recent Android or Galaxy phone and want a trusted brand. Skip it if you use an iPhone, since it will not pair.
pros: Single tag eases a first purchase
products.skipIf: You carry an iPhone or an older Android.

products.name: Life360 Tile Essentials Bluetooth Trackers
products.verdict: A Tile bundle for keys, wallets and remotes that works on both iOS and Android.
products.description:
Tile Essentials is Life360's bundle of Bluetooth trackers for keys, wallets, remotes and similar household items, working on both iOS and Android. The listing sits in the $50 to $100 bracket and does not publish a full spec sheet, so the pack contents are best confirmed on the product page.

It ranks third because cross-platform support is its strongest card. A household with an iPhone and an Android phone can run the same Tile app, which is simpler than juggling two ecosystems. The tradeoff is a smaller finding network than Apple's, and the sparse listing means you must read the page to learn exactly which tag shapes you get.

Pick it for a mixed family that wants one system for everything. Skip it if you want exact details before you buy, because this listing gives fewer.
pros: One app for iPhone and Android
products.skipIf: You want a fully detailed spec sheet.

products.name: UGREEN Finder Duo Air Tracker Tags 4 Pack
products.verdict: Four tags that the listing says work with both iOS and Android, at the $25 to $50 tier.
products.description:
The UGREEN Finder Duo Air is a four-tag set that the listing says supports both iOS and Android. It sits in the $25 to $50 bracket, so it is the cheapest set in this ranking.

It ranks fourth because four cross-platform tags for that price is a strong deal on paper, and UGREEN is a known accessories brand. It sits below Tile because Tile publishes more about its network and app, and the UGREEN listing is short on finding-network details. A multi-pack is also only useful if the app is reliable, which is hard to judge from a listing.

Buy it if you want many tags for little money and you carry either phone type. Skip it if network reach is your top priority, in which case the AirTag set is stronger.
pros: Four tags at a low price
cons: App quality is hard to judge
products.idealFor: Budget buyers who need many tags on any phone.
products.skipIf: You want the widest finding network.

products.name: Chipolo POP Tracking Tag
products.verdict: A colorful, loud tracker that is easy to hear when keys are buried in a bag.
products.description:
The Chipolo POP is a colorful tag pitched as a loud Bluetooth tracker, and this listing falls in the $50 to $100 bracket. It stresses compatibility and volume more than a spec list.

It ranks fifth because loudness is useful but is only one part of what a tracker does. In a big house a tag that rings clearly beats a quiet one by a wide margin, and color coding helps you keep several tags straight. It is placed below the UGREEN and Tile bundles because a single tag at this price offers less coverage than a multi-pack, and the listing is light on network detail.

Get it if you lose keys inside your home and want to hear them from another room. Skip it if you want one purchase to cover many items.
products.idealFor: People who misplace keys inside the house.
products.skipIf: You need to tag many items at once.

products.name: Samsung SmartTag2 Bluetooth + UWB 4-Pack Global Edition
products.verdict: IP67 rating and a 1.5 year battery, held back by a global edition with no US warranty.
products.description:
This four-pack SmartTag2 combines Bluetooth with UWB, carries an IP67 water and dust resistance rating, and lists a 1.5 year battery life. It is a global edition and the listing notes it has no US warranty, and it sits in the $50 to $100 bracket.

On raw specs it looks the best here: IP67 means it survives splashes and brief submersion, and UWB allows a more precise direction when you are close. It ranks last because a missing US warranty is a serious risk if a tag fails, and importing a global edition can bring surprises with app features. Its findable-via-app listing is also the same Samsung network, which is thinner than Apple's.

Buy it only if you want the ruggedness and accept the warranty gap. Otherwise the US-sold Samsung single tag is the safer route.
pros: IP67 rated for water and dust
cons: Global edition with no US warranty
products.idealFor: Rugged use by buyers who accept the warranty gap.
products.skipIf: A US warranty matters to you.

methodology.description: We checked each set against iOS, Android 11 and mixed-phone households, because compatibility decides whether a tracker works at all.

methodology.description: Single tags, four-packs and bundles were compared by how much coverage each gives inside the $25 to $50 and $50 to $100 brackets.

methodology.description: Water and dust ratings, battery life and rugged build were taken from the listings and weighed against the intended use.

methodology.title: Finding network
methodology.description: Apple's Find My, Samsung's network and Tile's were judged on likely reach, since an item can only be found if nearby devices detect it.

methodology.description: US warranty coverage and brand track record were weighed, including the risk of imported global editions.

whatMatters.factor: Which network will find your item
whatMatters.detail: A Bluetooth tag has no GPS of its own. It relies on nearby phones to relay its location, so the size of the crowd behind the network decides your odds. Apple has the largest crowd, Samsung's depends on Galaxy users and Tile's is open to iOS and Android. Read the listing for the named network.

whatMatters.factor: Pack size and cost per tag
whatMatters.detail: Four-packs cost far less per tag than singles, which is why the under $100 bracket is where multi-packs shine. Count what you actually lose: keys, a bag, a laptop, a suitcase. A pack of four is wasted if you will only ever tag one item.

An IP67 rating means a tag can survive dust and brief immersion, which matters on luggage and outdoor gear. Without a rating, treat a tag as splash-tolerant at best. Look for an IP code on the listing instead of the word waterproof.
Some tags use a replaceable coin cell and others have a sealed battery. A figure like 1.5 years gives you a replacement schedule. Choose a replaceable cell if you want to keep the tag for many years.

A global edition may lack US warranty coverage, as the Samsung 4-pack states. If a tag fails, you could have no recourse. Check for a US warranty line, and be careful with imports sold by third parties.

faq.q: Can I use a Samsung SmartTag2 with an iPhone?
faq.a: No. The SmartTag2 is built for Android 11 or later phones and tablets, and it cannot pair with iOS. iPhone owners should choose an AirTag or a cross-platform Tile.

faq.q: What mistake should I avoid when buying a four-pack?
faq.a: Buying more tags than you will use, or buying a set for the wrong phone. Count the items you lose, then confirm compatibility. Extra tags sitting in a drawer are wasted money.

faq.q: Is the AirTag four-pack worth it over a single?
faq.a: If you have three or more items to track, yes, because the cost per tag falls noticeably. For one set of keys, a single tag is enough. Most households end up using at least three.

faq.q: How do I set up several tags?
faq.a: Add them one at a time in the maker's app, naming each item as you go. Attach every tag before you pair the next one so you do not mix them up. Setup takes about a minute per tag.

faq.q: Should I worry about a missing US warranty?
faq.a: Yes, if you plan to use the tag for years. A global edition may not be covered if it fails, and returns can be harder. The US-sold Samsung single tag avoids that problem.

faq.q: Can these tags track a pet live?
faq.a: Not live. A Bluetooth tag shows only where a nearby phone last saw it. It can help find a pet that is close by, but a GPS collar is a better tool for a pet that roams.

finalTake: For an iPhone family, the Apple AirTag (2nd Generation) 4 Pack is the best Bluetooth tracker set under $100, thanks to its range and the Find My network. Android users should take the Samsung Galaxy SmartTag2, and mixed households are well served by the Tile Essentials bundle. The UGREEN four-pack is the cheapest way to tag many things, while the global Samsung pack is best avoided unless you accept the warranty gap. Match the set to your phones and you cannot go far wrong.
